claim: Spatial maps derived from band-specific local field potential (LFP) power can account for up to 90% of the spatial variability in RSNs derived from rsfMRI signals for both M1 and ACC recording sites.
source: Our data reveal that for both recording sites, spatial maps derived from band-specific local field potential (LFP) power can account for up to 90% of the spatial variability in RSNs derived from rsfMRI signals.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on the study's data analysis.

claim: The time series of LFP band power can only explain a maximum of 35% of the temporal variance of the local rsfMRI time course from the same site.
source: Surprisingly, the time series of LFP band power can only explain to a maximum of 35% of the temporal variance of the local rsfMRI time course from the same site.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the study's temporal correlation analysis.

claim: Regressing out time series of LFP power from rsfMRI signals has minimal impact on the spatial patterns of rsfMRI-based RSNs.
source: In addition, regressing out time series of LFP power from rsfMRI signals has minimal impact on the spatial patterns of rsfMRI-based RSNs.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding from regression analysis performed in the study.

claim: There exists an rsfMRI component contributed by 'electrophysiology-invisible' signals.
source: This disparity in the spatial and temporal relationships between resting-state electrophysiology and rsfMRI signals suggests that electrophysiological activity alone does not fully explain the effects observed in the rsfMRI signal, implying the existence of an rsfMRI component contributed by 'electrophysiology-invisible' signals.
evidence: The abstract explicitly proposes this interpretation based on the observed disparity in spatial and temporal relationships.

claim: The BOLD signal indirectly reflects neural activity through accompanying hemodynamic and metabolic changes via neurovascular coupling (NVC).
source: This is a fundamental issue, as the BOLD signal is known to indirectly reflect neural activity through accompanying hemodynamic and metabolic changes, a mechanism known as neurovascular coupling (NVC).
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding of BOLD signal mechanisms.

claim: Tight neurovascular coupling has been repeatedly demonstrated when neural activities are evoked by explicit external stimulation.
source: While tight NVC has been repeatedly demonstrated when neural activities are evoked by explicit external stimulation (Goense and Logothetis, 2008; Logothetis et al., 2001; Nemoto et al., 2004), this relationship in the resting state remains elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The spatial patterns of most RSNs effectively mirror established functional systems and activation patterns observed during various tasks.
source: There is considerable evidence indicating that the spatial patterns of most RSNs effectively mirror established functional systems and activation patterns observed during various tasks (Biswal et al., 1995; Glasser et al., 2016; Hampson et al., 2002; Lowe et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2009), as well as patterns of brain structural networks (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Greicius et al., 2009; Lowe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Alterations in RSNs have been documented in several brain disorders, aligning with neuropathophysiological changes.
source: In addition, alterations in RSNs have been documented in several brain disorders, aligning with neuropathophysiological changes (Buckner et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The predictive power of resting-state electrophysiological signals for corresponding rsfMRI time series is often relatively low.
source: However, it is notable that despite these findings, the predictive power of resting-state electrophysiological signals for corresponding rsfMRI time series is often relatively low (Mateo et al., 2017; Schölvinck et al., 2010; Winder et al., 2017), and some studies have even demonstrated a disconnection between neural activity and hemodynamic signals under specific conditions (Maier et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Various studies have reported divergent electrophysiological correlates of the rsfMRI signal across a broad spectrum of LFP bands.
source: Moreover, various studies have reported divergent electrophysiological correlates of the rsfMRI signal across a broad spectrum of LFP bands, spanning from infraslow signals (Hiltunen et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2013) and low-frequency delta/sub-delta band signals (He et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2007) to high-frequency gamma-band signals (Bastos et al., 2015; Foster et al., 2015; Keller et al., 2013; Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2008; Magri et al., 2012), as well as spiking activity (Mukamel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Simultaneous electrophysiology and rsfMRI recordings were conducted in the primary motor cortex (M1) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in rats under light sedation and wakefulness.
source: In conjunction with whole-brain rsfMRI, we simultaneously recorded electrophysiology signals in the primary motor cortex (M1) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in rats under light sedation and wakefulness.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: M1 and ACC were chosen as recording sites due to their distinct roles in sensorimotor function and integrative cognition, respectively.
source: These brain regions were chosen due to their distinct roles in sensorimotor function and integrative cognition, respectively.
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting these specific brain regions.

claim: In both light-sedation and awake states, the spatial patterns of RSNs derived from gamma-band power closely resemble BOLD-derived RSNs for both M1 and ACC.
source: Our data show that in both light-sedation and awake states, the spatial patterns of RSNs derived from gamma-band power closely resemble BOLD-derived RSNs for both the M1 and ACC, and lower-frequency band-derived RSNs exhibit inversed spatial patterns, both indicating strong neural underpinning of RSNs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings from data analysis.

claim: Lower-frequency band-derived RSNs exhibit inversed spatial patterns compared to BOLD-derived RSNs.
source: Our data show that in both light-sedation and awake states, the spatial patterns of RSNs derived from gamma-band power closely resemble BOLD-derived RSNs for both the M1 and ACC, and lower-frequency band-derived RSNs exhibit inversed spatial patterns, both indicating strong neural underpinning of RSNs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings from data analysis.

claim: The temporal profiles of band-limited LFP powers at both recording sites exhibit considerably lower temporal correlations with the corresponding local BOLD time courses.
source: However, the temporal profiles of band-limited LFP powers at both recording sites exhibit considerably lower temporal correlations with the corresponding local BOLD time courses.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings from temporal correlation analysis.

claim: Gamma-band power is positively correlated with the BOLD signal.
source: These data demonstrate that gamma-band power is positively correlated with the BOLD signal, while lower-frequency bands display negative peak correlations with the BOLD signal.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lower-frequency bands display negative peak correlations with the BOLD signal.
source: These data demonstrate that gamma-band power is positively correlated with the BOLD signal, while lower-frequency bands display negative peak correlations with the BOLD signal.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lag of the BOLD signal is approximately 2 s for all LFP bands.
source: Additionally, the lag of the BOLD signal is approximately 2 s for all bands, consistent with the hemodynamic response function (HRF) delay previously reported in rodents (Schölvinck et al., 2010; Winder et al., 2017).
evidence: This finding is stated and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For M1, the voxel-to-voxel Pearson correlation coefficient between the mean gamma-derived RSN map and mean BOLD-derived RSN map was 0.95.
source: Specifically, for M1, the voxel-to-voxel Pearson correlation coefficient (CC) between the mean gamma-derived RSN map (Figure 1E) and mean BOLD-derived RSN map (Figure 1F) was 0.95 (Figure 1K, R2=0.90), indicating 90% of the variance in the M1 BOLD-derived RSN map could be explained by the gamma-derived map.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from spatial correlation analysis, with reference to specific figures.

claim: 90% of the variance in the M1 BOLD-derived RSN map could be explained by the gamma-derived map.
source: Specifically, for M1, the voxel-to-voxel Pearson correlation coefficient (CC) between the mean gamma-derived RSN map (Figure 1E) and mean BOLD-derived RSN map (Figure 1F) was 0.95 (Figure 1K, R2=0.90), indicating 90% of the variance in the M1 BOLD-derived RSN map could be explained by the gamma-derived map.
evidence: This is derived from the R-squared value of the spatial correlation analysis.

claim: Spatial maps generated by lower-frequency bands displayed inverse correlations with the M1 BOLD-derived RSN map.
source: Conversely, spatial maps generated by lower-frequency bands displayed inverse correlations with the M1 BOLD-derived RSN map, with a trend of increasingly negative spatial CC in lower-frequency bands (Figure 1E–J, delta: CC = –0.78; theta: CC = –0.78; alpha: CC = –0.5; beta: CC = –0.34), consistent with the LFP-BOLD cross correlations for these bands shown in Figure 1B and C.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from spatial correlation analysis with specific correlation coefficients provided.

claim: For ACC, the spatial correlation between gamma-derived and BOLD-derived RSN maps was 0.85.
source: These relationships are repeatable in the ACC (Figure 2A–G, delta: CC = –0.62; theta: CC = –0.3; alpha: CC = –0.12; beta: CC = 0.12; gamma: CC = 0.85).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from spatial correlation analysis for the ACC region.

claim: The spatial patterns of BOLD-based RSNs can be reliably obtained using band-specific LFP signals.
source: These results suggest that the spatial patterns of BOLD-based RSNs can be reliably obtained using band-specific LFP signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial correlation analysis results.

claim: In M1, the LFP-BOLD temporal correlations gradually shifted from negative to positive as the LFP signal transitioned from low to high frequencies.
source: In the M1, the LFP-BOLD temporal correlations gradually shifted from negative to positive as the LFP signal transitioned from low to high frequencies, mirroring the trend observed in spatial correlations (Figure 1E–K).
evidence: This describes the pattern observed in temporal correlation analysis.

claim: The absolute magnitude of temporal correlations between LFP and BOLD was considerably lower than spatial correlations, despite being statistically significant.
source: However, the absolute magnitude of these CCs was considerably lower, despite that they were all statistically significant (one-sample t-tests, delta: CC = –0.20, p=2.1 × 10–57; theta: CC = –0.19, p=7.1 × 10–62; alpha: CC = –0.11, p=1.2 × 10–42; beta: CC = –0.06, p=8.4 × 10–15; gamma: CC = 0.37; p=2.1 × 10–58; number of scans = 159).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: Similar temporal correlation results were observed in the ACC as in M1.
source: Similar results were observed in the ACC (one-sample t-tests; delta: CC = –0.13, p=1.9 × 10–28; theta: CC = –0.04, p=8.4 × 10–7; alpha: CC = –0.03, p=6.0 × 10–5; beta: CC = –0.01, p=0.1; gamma: CC = 0.18, p=6.7 × 10–42; number of scans = 172).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis for the ACC region.

claim: The magnitude of spatial correlations remains appreciably higher than that of temporal correlations for all bands even after controlling for variance level.
source: Comparisons of scan-wise spatial and temporal correlations (Figure 3A and B) indicate that even after controlling for the variance level, the magnitude of spatial correlations remains appreciably higher than that of temporal correlations for all bands (paired t-tests across individual scans; in the M1, delta: p=1.01 × 10–35; theta: p=3.74 × 10–50; alpha: p=3.54 × 10–25; beta: p=1.18 × 10–12; gamma: p=7.02 × 10–42; in the ACC, delta: p=6.73 × 10–21; theta: p=5.75 × 10–5; alpha: p=0.74; beta: p=7.34 × 10–5; gamma: p=3.43 × 10–29).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical comparison of spatial and temporal correlations.

claim: The true BOLD-LFP temporal correlation in M1 is estimated to be approximately 0.59 (R²=0.35) after accounting for noise effects.
source: At this CNR level, we estimated that the true BOLD-LFP temporal correlation in the M1 should be approximately 0.59 (R2=0.35, Figure 3F and G), when the apparent correlation is 0.37 as measured by the gamma-BOLD temporal correlation in our real data (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an estimate derived from simulation analysis to account for noise effects.

claim: The temporal information provided by gamma power can only explain approximately 35% of the temporal variance in the BOLD time series after accounting for noise effect.
source: These findings indicate the temporal information provided by gamma power can only explain a minor portion (approximately 35%) of the temporal variance in the BOLD time series, even after accounting for the noise effect, which is in line with the reported correlation values between the cerebral blood volume (CBV) and fluctuations in GCaMP signal in head-fixed mice during periods of immobility (R=0.63) (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation analysis, supported by comparison to previous research.

claim: The difference in the number of data points (1200 in temporal correlation calculation vs. 6157 in spatial correlation calculation) has a negligible influence on correlation values.
source: Furthermore, our simulation suggests that the difference in the number of data points (1200 in temporal correlation calculation vs. 6157 in spatial correlation calculation) has a negligible influence on correlation values (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: After regressing out gamma-band power from M1, the spatial patterns of gamma power-derived RSN maps disappeared.
source: As expected, the spatial patterns of gamma power-derived RSN maps observed in Figures 1E and 2A disappeared after the regression (Figures 4A and 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis.

claim: Regressing out gamma-band power minimally altered M1/ACC BOLD-derived RSN maps.
source: However, this regression process minimally altered M1/ACC BOLD-derived RSN maps (Figures 4B and 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis.

claim: The result that regression minimally alters RSN maps remained consistent when the powers of all LFP bands were voxel-wise regressed out from rsfMRI signals using soft regression.
source: This result remained consistent when the powers of all LFP bands were voxel-wise regressed out from rsfMRI signals using soft regression (Figures 4C and 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the soft regression analysis.

claim: Soft regression was utilized to address the multicollinearity issue in the regression model resulting from potential correlations between LFP bands.
source: Soft regression was utilized to address the multicollinearity issue in the regression model resulting from potential correlations between LFP bands, as this method allows only unique components in five LFP bands to be regressed out.
evidence: This explains the methodological choice for the regression analysis.

claim: The removal of gamma power has limited impact on the M1/ACC RSN maps.
source: The spatial similarities between the BOLD-derived RSN maps before and after gamma power regression, all band power regression, or peak removal are summarized in Figures 4F and 5E, showing that the removal of gamma power has limited impact on the M1/ACC RSN maps.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of RSN maps after various regression procedures.

claim: The nonlinear component between BOLD and electrophysiological signals, reflected by mutual information, does not significantly influence RSN spatial patterns.
source: The results show limited mutual information between any band-specific power and voxel-wise rsfMRI signals, indicating that the nonlinear component between BOLD and electrophysiological signals, reflected by mutual information, does not significantly influence RSN spatial patterns, which is consistent with the report that macroscopic resting-state brain dynamics are best described by linear models (Nozari et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a finding from mutual information analysis, supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The temporal fluctuations of LFP have limited effects on BOLD-derived RSN spatial patterns.
source: These data collectively indicate that the temporal fluctuations of LFP have limited effects on BOLD-derived RSN spatial patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regression and mutual information analyses.

claim: The disparity between temporal and spatial correlations of resting-state LFP and fMRI signals persists in awake rats.
source: To determine whether the disparity between temporal and spatial correlations of resting-state LFP and fMRI signals we observed is a specific phenomenon under anesthesia or can be generalized to different physiological states, we repeated the experiment in awake rats.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to test generalizability across physiological states.

claim: Higher spatial correlations between LFP-derived maps and BOLD-derived RSN maps were found in awake rats in M1.
source: Despite that the physiological dynamics are substantially different, we still found higher spatial correlations between LFP-derived maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) and the BOLD-derived RSN map (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) in the M1.
evidence: This is a finding from the awake rat experiments.

claim: Significant but weaker temporal correlations between the rsfMRI signal and HRF-convolved gamma-band power were observed in awake rats.
source: Similar to the results in Figure 3, significant but weaker temporal correlations between the rsfMRI signal and HRF-convolved gamma-band power were observed in awake rats (one-sample t-tests; for M1, delta: CC = –0.05, p=2.3 × 10–4; theta: CC = –0.06, p=4.7 × 10–6; alpha: CC = –0.06, p=4.6 × 10–5; beta: CC = –0.032, p=3.0 × 10–3; gamma: CC = 0.04, p=0.02; for ACC, delta: CC = 0.02, p=0.29; theta: CC = 0.0009, p=0.96; alpha: CC = –0.02, p=0.31; beta: CC = 0.006, p=0.66; gamma: CC = 0.10, p=9.52 × 10–7; number of scans = 50).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis in awake rats.

claim: Both spatial and temporal correlations showed lower magnitudes in the awake state compared to light-sedation state.
source: Overall, both spatial and temporal correlations showed lower magnitudes in the awake state, likely due to increased variability from motion and other physiological fluctuations, as well as the smaller number of scans compared to the light-sedation state (50 awake scans, 159 light-sedation scans for M1, and 172 light-sedation scans for ACC).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing results across physiological states with a proposed explanation.

claim: The consistent pattern of lower temporal but higher spatial correlations between gamma power and the rsfMRI signal supports the notion that this disparity is a general phenomenon across different physiological states.
source: Nonetheless, the consistent pattern of lower temporal but higher spatial correlations between gamma power and the rsfMRI signal supports the notion that this disparity is a general phenomenon across different physiological states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing results across physiological states.

claim: The lack of significant alteration in BOLD-derived RSN maps after regressing out gamma-band power or powers of all LFP bands in both ACC and M1 of awake rats reinforces earlier findings.
source: The lack of significant alteration in BOLD-derived RSN maps after regressing out gamma-band power or powers of all LFP bands in both ACC and M1 of awake rats (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) further reinforces our earlier findings.
evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis in awake rats.

claim: The major findings observed in lightly anesthetized rats can be replicated in unanesthetized rats.
source: These results indicate that the major findings observed in lightly anesthetized rats, including the disparity between temporal and spatial correlations, can be replicated in unanesthetized rats.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing results across anesthetized and awake states.

claim: The findings are not specific to the effects of anesthesia but rather reflect fundamental aspects of the relationship between electrophysiological and hemodynamic signals in the brain across different physiological states.
source: Therefore, it appears that these results are not specific to the effects of anesthesia but rather reflect fundamental aspects of the relationship between electrophysiological and hemodynamic signals in the brain across different physiological states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistency of findings across physiological states.

claim: Brain activity consists of components measurable by electrophysiology and others that are electrophysiology-invisible.
source: Brain activity consists of components measurable by electrophysiology and others that are electrophysiology-invisible.
evidence: This is a statement from the proposed theoretical model.

claim: Electrophysiology-invisible brain activities, such as those involving nNOS neurons and astrocytes, actively contribute to NVC and can exert a significant influence on the rsfMRI signal.
source: In addition to the electrophysiology activity, electrophysiology-invisible brain activities, such as those involving nNOS neurons and astrocytes, actively contribute to NVC and can exert a significant influence on the rsfMRI signal.
evidence: This is a statement from the proposed theoretical model.

claim: During the resting state, electrophysiology and electrophysiology-invisible components may not be synchronized, lowering temporal correlations between electrophysiology and rsfMRI signals.
source: During the resting state, these two components may not be synchronized, lowering temporal correlations between electrophysiology and rsfMRI signals.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the theoretical model to explain the observed disparity.

claim: Neuromodulations from distal modulator nuclei (e.g. locus coerulues and/or basal forebrain) could contribute to low LFP-BOLD temporal correlations by exerting strong vasoactive effects that may not proportionately affect electrophysiology activity.
source: Another factor contributing to low LFP-BOLD temporal correlations could be neuromodulations from distal modulator nuclei (e.g. locus coerulues and/or basal forebrain), which exert strong vasoactive effects but may not proportionately affect electrophysiology activity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the theoretical model to explain the observed disparity.

claim: The signaling of electrophysiology activities and that of electrophysiology-invisible components are both constrained by the same anatomical pathways.
source: Moreover, the signaling of electrophysiology activities and that of electrophysiology-invisible are both constrained by the same anatomical pathways.
evidence: This is a statement from the proposed theoretical model.

claim: Anatomical constraints allow electrophysiology and electrophysiology-invisible signals to generate similar RSN spatial patterns in parallel measured by the BOLD signal.
source: This allows the two signals to generate similar RSN spatial patterns in parallel measured by the BOLD signal, which can reflect both direct and indirect anatomical connectivity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the theoretical model to explain high spatial correlations.

claim: BOLD-derived RSNs have been widely investigated in multiple species.
source: BOLD-derived RSNs have been widely investigated in multiple species (Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2012; Mantini et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2011) and have been applied in various physiological and pathological conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies employing electroencephalography or electrocorticography in humans have shown that RSNs derived from the power of multiple-site electrophysiological signals exhibit similar spatial patterns to classic BOLD-derived RSNs.
source: Studies employing electroencephalography or electrocorticography in humans have shown that RSNs derived from the power of multiple-site electrophysiological signals exhibit similar spatial patterns to classic BOLD-derived RSNs, such as the default-mode network (Hacker et al., 2017; Kucyi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High spatial correspondence between rsfMRI and LFP signals can be found at the columnar level.
source: This high spatial correspondence between rsfMRI and LFP signals can even be found at the columnar level (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Simultaneous recordings of resting-state calcium and fMRI signals in awake rats have revealed highly consistent spatial patterns between calcium- and BOLD-associated RSNs.
source: Similarly, simultaneous recordings of resting-state calcium and fMRI signals in awake rats have revealed highly consistent spatial patterns between calcium- and BOLD-associated RSNs (Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Voltage-sensitive dye imaging in mice has unveiled comparable sensory-evoked and hemisphere-wide activity motifs represented in spontaneous activity in both lightly anesthetized and awake states.
source: Moreover, voltage-sensitive dye imaging in mice has unveiled comparable sensory-evoked and hemisphere-wide activity motifs represented in spontaneous activity in both lightly anesthetized and awake states (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Overlapping cortical networks were identified using both fMRI and calcium imaging modalities, suggesting that networks observable in fMRI studies exhibit corresponding neural activity spatial patterns.
source: Furthermore, in a more recent study by Vafaii and colleagues, overlapping cortical networks were identified using both fMRI and calcium imaging modalities, suggesting that networks observable in fMRI studies exhibit corresponding neural activity spatial patterns (Vafaii et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Consistent sensory-evoked and hemisphere-wide activity motifs in mice, as revealed using voltage-sensitive dye imaging, are defined by regional axonal projections.
source: For instance, consistent sensory-evoked and hemisphere-wide activity motifs in mice, as revealed using voltage-sensitive dye imaging, are defined by regional axonal projections (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous work in awake rats demonstrates spatial consistency between RSNs and anatomical connectivity patterns in thalamocortical networks.
source: Our previous work in awake rats further demonstrate spatial consistency between RSNs and anatomical connectivity patterns in thalamocortical networks (Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: RSNs revealed by either the BOLD or LFP signal closely resemble the corresponding anatomical networks from the Allen Brain Institute database.
source: In the current study, we compared RSNs of M1 and ACC to their anatomical networks defined by the axonal projection patterns obtained from the Allen Brain Institute database (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Oh et al., 2014), illustrating that RSNs revealed by either the BOLD or LFP signal closely resemble the corresponding anatomical networks.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing RSNs to anatomical data, supported by citation.

claim: RSNs measured by functional connectivity can reflect both direct and indirect connectivity and thus may not necessarily have identical spatial patterns as the corresponding anatomical networks.
source: It is important to note that RSNs measured by functional connectivity can reflect both direct and indirect connectivity and thus may not necessarily have identical spatial patterns as the corresponding anatomical networks (Honey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous research demonstrated weak but significant correlations between CBV changes and spontaneous gamma-band LFP or multiunit activity in awake, head-fixed mice.
source: These results are supported by previous research demonstrating weak but significant correlations between CBV changes and spontaneous gamma-band LFP or multiunit activity in awake, head-fixed mice (Winder et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Persistent spontaneous fluctuations in CBV were observed even after blocking local neural spiking and glutamatergic input, as well as noradrenergic receptors.
source: Importantly, persistent spontaneous fluctuations in CBV were observed even after blocking local neural spiking and glutamatergic input, as well as noradrenergic receptors, indicating that hemodynamic signal fluctuations may not dominantly reflect local ongoing electrophysiology activity (Winder et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Comparably low temporal correlations between gamma-band power and the rsfMRI signal have been reported in monkeys.
source: Comparably low temporal correlations between gamma-band power and the rsfMRI signal have been reported in monkeys (Schölvinck et al., 2010; Shmuel and Leopold, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Data from the authors' group show similarly low temporal correlations between spontaneous calcium peaks and the rsfMRI signal in awake rats.
source: Additionally, data from our group show similarly low temporal correlations between spontaneous calcium peaks, a measure of neural spiking activity, and the rsfMRI signal in awake rats (Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Vafaii et al. revealed notable differences in functional connectivity strength measured by fMRI and calcium imaging, despite an overlapping spatial pattern of cortical networks identified by both modalities.
source: Furthermore, Vafaii et al. revealed notable differences in functional connectivity strength measured by fMRI and calcium imaging, despite an overlapping spatial pattern of cortical networks identified by both modalities (Vafaii et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The temporal correlation between electrophysiology and rsfMRI signals is significant, but the effect size of this correlation might be small.
source: These findings collectively suggest that while the temporal correlation between electrophysiology and rsfMRI signals is significant, the effect size of this correlation might be small.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: In M1, the temporal correlation between infraslow LFP power and the rsfMRI signal was 0.08, while both derived consistent RSN spatial patterns (spatial correlation = 0.7).
source: Our data show that in the M1, the temporal correlation between infraslow LFP power and the rsfMRI signal was 0.08, while both derived consistent RSN spatial patterns (spatial correlation = 0.7), in line with the report that RSNs can be derived from infraslow LFP activity (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of infraslow LFP activity, supported by citation.

claim: Two earlier studies in isoflurane-anesthetized rats found the LFP power in the primary somatosensory cortex was highly correlated with BOLD fluctuations.
source: It is noteworthy that these results differ from two earlier studies in isoflurane-anesthetized rats, which found the LFP power in the primary somatosensory cortex was highly correlated with BOLD fluctuations (Liu et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The discrepancy with earlier studies may be attributed to brain-wide synchronization during burst suppression in deeply anesthetized states.
source: This discrepancy may be attributed to brain-wide synchronization during burst suppression in deeply anesthetized states in those studies.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for differences with previous research.

claim: LFP records various neural activities, such as synaptic potentials and voltage-gated membrane fluctuations, reflecting the input and local neural processing of a particular brain region.
source: LFP records various neural activities, such as synaptic potentials and voltage-gated membrane fluctuations, reflecting the input and local neural processing of a particular brain region.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about LFP recordings.

claim: Electrophysiology cannot measure activities from certain cell populations, while electrophysiology-invisible components can trigger vasoactive responses and significantly contribute to the rsfMRI signal.
source: However, electrophysiology cannot measure activities from certain cell populations, while electrophysiology-invisible components can trigger vasoactive responses and significantly contribute to the rsfMRI signal.
evidence: This is a statement from the discussion explaining limitations of electrophysiology.

claim: The electrical activity of nNOS neurons is not detectable by electrophysiology because the nNOS neuron population is very small, yet it strongly contributes to NVC.
source: For instance, the electrical activity of nNOS neurons is not detectable by electrophysiology because the nNOS neuron population is very small, yet it strongly contributes to NVC.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about nNOS neurons.

claim: Chemogenetic or pharmacological stimulation of nNOS neurons causes vasodilation without detectable changes in LFP.
source: Chemogenetic or pharmacological stimulation of nNOS neurons causes vasodilation without detectable changes in LFP (Echagarruga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Astrocytes coordinate communication between neurons and blood vessels and play a crucial role in NVC.
source: In addition, astrocytes, a type of glia cell, coordinate communication between neurons and blood vessels and play a crucial role in NVC.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about astrocytes.

claim: Astrocytes regulate vessel tone by releasing signaling molecules such as ATP, arachidonic acid metabolites, and nitric oxide.
source: Astrocytes regulate vessel tone by releasing signaling molecules such as ATP, arachidonic acid metabolites, and nitric oxide (Iadecola and Nedergaard, 2007; Mulligan and MacVicar, 2004; Murphy et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Astrocytes can alter the diameter of blood vessels by extending or retracting the endfeet wrapping around them.
source: Furthermore, astrocytes can alter the diameter of blood vessels by extending or retracting the endfeet wrapping around them (Mills et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of astrocytes in transgenic mice without affecting neurons elicited a BOLD response, indicating that astrocyte activity alone can cause changes in the BOLD signal, independent of neuronal activity.

claim: Band-specific LFP power was computed using a conventional LFP band definition (delta: 1–4 Hz, theta: 4–7 Hz, alpha: 7–13 Hz, beta: 13–30 Hz, gamma: 40–100 Hz).
source: Based on the conventional LFP band definition (delta: 1–4 Hz, theta: 4–7 Hz, alpha: 7–13 Hz, beta: 13–30 Hz, gamma: 40–100 Hz) (Lu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020), the LFP band power was computed using the MATLAB function spectrogram with a window size of 1 s and a step size of 0.1 s.
evidence: This describes the method for computing band-specific LFP power, supported by citations.

claim: The time course of band-specific LFP power was convolved with a rodent-specific HRF to generate the corresponding LFP-predicted BOLD signal.
source: To investigate the relationship between the LFP and rsfMRI signals, the time course of band-specific LFP power was convolved with an HRF (p = [4 4 1 1 6 0 32] for function spm_hrf) to generate the corresponding LFP-predicted BOLD signal. The HRF used was specific to rodents with a shorter onset time and time-to-peak as a faster HRF was reported in rats relative to humans (Tong et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the method for generating LFP-predicted BOLD signals, supported by citation.
